steps.say: Now the heel, same weight but a tiny area:

Same person, same weight, but the heel presses 6000 on each square metre against the snowshoe's 30. That force-per-area is exactly pressure, \(p = \frac{F}{A}\). Small area, big pressure, which is why a heel dents a floor a boot never would. Liquids do the same with depth: \(p = h\rho g\).

Same 60 N of weight, two different shoes:

steps: Identify which equation: p = F/A (solid on a surface) or p = hρg (liquid at depth)
Convert units first: cm to m (÷100), cm² to m² (÷10,000)
State the answer with its unit; for total pressure at depth, add atmospheric pressure
method_card.title: Pressure in Fluids
method_card.content:
Two pressure equations, and you must choose the right one.

Solid on a surface: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\). The force is the object's weight; the area is the contact face. For maximum pressure, use the smallest face.

Liquid at depth: \(p = h\rho g\). Depth in metres, density in kg/m³.

Watch the units: cm to m divide by 100; cm² to m² divide by 10,000. For total pressure in a liquid, add atmospheric pressure (about 101,000 Pa) to the liquid pressure. Remember 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.

steps: Two moves chained. Total pressure at depth: work out the liquid pressure \(h\rho g\), then ADD atmospheric pressure (about 101,000 Pa).
Or find a force from a pressure: \(p = h\rho g\) first, then \(F = p \times A\).
Keep units consistent all the way through and state the final unit.
gold.title: Gold: more than one step

example.question: A submarine is 30 m deep in seawater (1025 kg/m³). Atmospheric pressure is 101,000 Pa, g = 9.8. Find the total pressure.

steps: Pick the right equation. Solid pressing on a surface: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\). Liquid at depth: \(p = h\rho g\).
The values are already in the right units (N, m², m, kg/m³). Substitute and calculate in one go.
State the answer with its unit, usually pascals (Pa).
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in

example.question: A crate weighs 240 N and its base covers 0.06 m². Find the pressure.

steps: Same equations, but a value is in the wrong unit. Convert before you substitute: cm to m (÷100), cm² to m² (÷10,000).
Or the unknown is not the subject: rearrange first, for example \(h = \frac{p}{\rho g}\).
Then it is a bronze question: substitute and state the unit.

exam_context.frequency: Common, pressure appears on most Paper 1 exams

gold.hint: Find the liquid pressure with hρg, then add atmospheric pressure.
gold.display: A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea (density 1025 kg/m³). Calculate the total pressure on the diver. Atmospheric pressure = 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two steps: liquid pressure with \(h\rho g\), then add atmospheric pressure.

guided_steps.pre: Density of seawater in kg/m³: ρ =

guided_steps.say: Add atmospheric pressure.
guided_steps.hint: Add the air's pressure on top.

guided_steps.done: That is the water's share, so total = 352,125 Pa.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract atmospheric to get the liquid pressure back.

misconceptions.message: Add atmospheric pressure: total = 251,125 + 101,000 = 352,125 Pa. The liquid pressure alone is 251,125.
Use seawater density 1025 kg/m³, not 1000. Liquid pressure = 25 × 1025 × 9.8 = 251,125 Pa, total 352,125 Pa. Fresh water gives 346,000.

gold.hint: Weight first, then divide by the smallest face for maximum pressure.
gold.display: A cuboid of mass 20 kg has dimensions 0.5 m × 0.2 m × 0.1 m. Calculate the maximum pressure it can exert on the floor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Maximum pressure needs the smallest face. First find the weight, then divide by the smallest area.
Divide weight by the smallest face.

guided_steps.done: Back to 196 N, so p = 9800 Pa.

misconceptions.message: For MAXIMUM pressure use the SMALLEST face (0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m²): p = 196 ÷ 0.02 = 9800 Pa. The largest face (0.1 m²) gives 1960.
Use the weight, not the mass: weight = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N, then p = 196 ÷ 0.02 = 9800 Pa. Using 20 N gives 1000.

gold.hint: Find the pressure at 40 m, then multiply by the gate area.
gold.display: A dam holds back water 40 m deep. Calculate the force on a gate at the bottom of the dam that is 2 m wide and 1.5 m tall. Use the pressure at the full 40 m depth. (density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two steps: pressure at 40 m with \(h\rho g\), then force with \(F = p \times A\).
Multiply pressure by the gate area.

misconceptions.message: Multiply the pressure by the gate area: F = 392,000 × 3 = 1,176,000 N. Stopping at the pressure gives 392,000.

gold.hint: Pressure is the same in the fluid: find it from the small piston, then F = p × A.
gold.display: In a hydraulic system, the small piston has an area of 0.002 m² and the large piston has an area of 0.04 m². A force of 50 N is applied to the small piston. Calculate the force exerted by the large piston.

guided_steps.say: Pressure is the same everywhere in the fluid. Find it from the small piston, then use \(F = p \times A\) on the large one.

guided_steps.hint: F ÷ A on the small piston.

guided_steps.pre: Large piston area in m²: A =

guided_steps.say: Multiply that pressure by the large area.

guided_steps.done: Same fluid pressure, so F = 1000 N.
guided_steps.hint: Force ÷ area gives the pressure back.

misconceptions.message: The large piston has the larger area, so the force is multiplied: F = 50 × (0.04 ÷ 0.002) = 1000 N. Inverting the ratio gives 2.5.

gold.hint: Rearrange p = hρg to h = p ÷ (ρg).
gold.display: A tank contains oil with a density of 800 kg/m³. At what depth does the pressure due to the oil equal atmospheric pressure (101,000 Pa)? Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(p = h\rho g\) to \(h = \frac{p}{\rho g}\). The answer is to 1 decimal place.
Divide the pressure by ρg and round to 1 d.p.

guided_steps.done: About 101,000 Pa, so h = 12.9 m to 1 d.p.
guided_steps.hint: Depth × ρg should return the pressure.

misconceptions.message: Use the density of oil (800 kg/m³): h = 101,000 ÷ (800 × 9.8) = 12.9 m. Using water (1000) gives 10.3.
Divide by ρg, not just ρ: h = 101,000 ÷ 7840 = 12.9 m. Dividing by 800 alone gives 126.25.

gold.hint: Find total pressure in Pa, then divide by 1000 for kPa.
gold.display: A submarine is 200 m below the surface of the sea (density of seawater = 1025 kg/m³). Calculate the total pressure on the hull in kPa. Atmospheric pressure = 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Total pressure in Pa first, then convert to kPa by dividing by 1000.
Add atmospheric pressure.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2,110,000 Pa, so total = 2110 kPa.

misconceptions.message: Add atmospheric pressure before converting: 2,009,000 + 101,000 = 2,110,000 Pa = 2110 kPa. The liquid pressure alone is 2009 kPa.
Convert Pa to kPa by dividing by 1000: 2,110,000 Pa = 2110 kPa. Leaving it in Pa gives 2,110,000.

bronze.hint: Pressure is force divided by area.
bronze.display: A box weighing 200 N rests on the floor. The area of the base is 0.04 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor.

guided_steps.say: Pressure is how hard a force presses on each bit of area: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\).

guided_steps.hint: Read the box's weight straight from the question.
It is already in m², no conversion needed.

guided_steps.say: Now divide force by area.
guided_steps.hint: Dividing by 0.04 is the same as ×25.

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 N, so p = 5000 Pa.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply your pressure by the area.

misconceptions.message: Pressure = force ÷ area, not force × area. 200 ÷ 0.04 = 5000 Pa.

bronze.hint: Liquid pressure is depth × density × g.
bronze.display: Calculate the pressure at the bottom of a 2 m deep swimming pool. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Liquid pressure grows with depth: \(p = h\rho g\).
Multiply depth × density × g, with g = 9.8.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 m, so p = 19,600 Pa.

bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Do not forget g. p = hρg = 2 × 1000 × 9.8 = 19,600 Pa. Leaving out g gives 2000.

bronze.display: A pressure of 60,000 Pa acts over an area of 0.1 m². Calculate the force.

guided_steps.say: To get force from pressure: \(F = p \times A\).
Multiply pressure by area.

guided_steps.done: Back to 60,000 Pa, so F = 6000 N.

misconceptions.message: Force = pressure × area = 60,000 × 0.1 = 6000 N. Dividing (60,000 ÷ 0.1 = 600,000) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Pressure is force divided by area.
bronze.display: A crate weighing 500 N rests on the ground with a base area of 0.05 m². Calculate the pressure.

guided_steps.say: Use \(p = \frac{F}{A}\).
Divide force by area.

guided_steps.done: Back to 500 N, so p = 10,000 Pa.

misconceptions.message: Pressure = force ÷ area = 500 ÷ 0.05 = 10,000 Pa. Multiplying (500 × 0.05 = 25) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Use p = hρg for liquid depth.
bronze.display: Calculate the pressure at a depth of 5 m in water. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: \(p = h\rho g\) for a liquid.
Multiply depth × density × g.

guided_steps.done: Back to 5 m, so p = 49,000 Pa.

bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Multiply by g as well: p = 5 × 1000 × 9.8 = 49,000 Pa. Leaving out g gives 5000.

bronze.hint: Area is force divided by pressure.
bronze.display: A 600 N force creates a pressure of 3000 Pa. Calculate the area over which it acts.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(p = \frac{F}{A}\) to \(A = \frac{F}{p}\).
Divide force by pressure.

guided_steps.done: Back to 3000 Pa, so A = 0.2 m².
guided_steps.hint: Force ÷ area should give the pressure.

misconceptions.message: Area = force ÷ pressure = 600 ÷ 3000 = 0.2 m². Dividing the other way (3000 ÷ 600 = 5) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Rearrange p = hρg to h = p ÷ (ρg).
bronze.display: The pressure at the bottom of a column of liquid is 29,400 Pa. The density is 1000 kg/m³. Calculate the depth. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(p = h\rho g\) to \(h = \frac{p}{\rho g}\).
Divide pressure by ρg.

guided_steps.done: Back to 29,400 Pa, so h = 3 m.

misconceptions.message: Divide by ρg, not just ρ: h = 29,400 ÷ (1000 × 9.8) = 29,400 ÷ 9800 = 3 m. Dividing by 1000 alone gives 29.4.

bronze.display: A pressure of 800 Pa acts on an area of 0.5 m². Calculate the force.

guided_steps.say: \(F = p \times A\).
Multiply pressure by area.

guided_steps.done: Back to 800 Pa, so F = 400 N.

misconceptions.message: Force = pressure × area = 800 × 0.5 = 400 N. Dividing (800 ÷ 0.5 = 1600) is the slip.

silver.hint: Convert both sides to metres before finding the area.
silver.display: A person weighing 300 N stands on a surface 20 cm × 50 cm. Calculate the pressure in Pa. (Give your answer as a whole number.)

guided_steps.say: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\), but the sides are in centimetres, so convert first.
Now use p = F/A.

guided_steps.done: Back to 300 N, so p = 3000 Pa.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m first: 0.2 m × 0.5 m = 0.1 m². Pressure = 300 ÷ 0.1 = 3000 Pa. Using cm (area 1000) gives 0.3.

silver.hint: Use the density of mercury, then p = hρg.
silver.display: A column of mercury (density 13,600 kg/m³) is 0.8 m tall. Calculate the pressure at the bottom in Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: \(p = h\rho g\). The twist is the density: use mercury, not water.

guided_steps.pre: Density of mercury in kg/m³: ρ =

guided_steps.say: Multiply depth × density × g.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.8 m, so p = 106,624 Pa.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Use the density of mercury (13,600 kg/m³), not water. p = 0.8 × 13,600 × 9.8 = 106,624 Pa. Water gives 7840.

silver.hint: Work out the liquid pressure, then add atmospheric pressure.
silver.display: Calculate the total pressure on a diver at 10 m depth in water (density 1000 kg/m³). Include atmospheric pressure of 101,000 Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Total pressure is the water's pressure PLUS the air pushing down: \(p_{\text{total}} = h\rho g + p_{\text{atm}}\).
Add atmospheric pressure.
guided_steps.hint: Add the air's pressure on top.

guided_steps.done: That is the water's share, so total = 199,000 Pa.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract atmospheric to get the liquid pressure back.

misconceptions.message: Add atmospheric pressure too: total = 98,000 + 101,000 = 199,000 Pa. The liquid pressure alone is 98,000.

silver.hint: Convert cm² to m² by dividing by 10,000.
silver.display: A nail pushes with a force of 50 N. The point of the nail has an area of 2 cm². Calculate the pressure in Pa.

guided_steps.say: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\), but the area is in cm², so convert to m² first.

guided_steps.pre: 1 m² = 10,000 cm², so 2 cm² in m² = 2 ÷ 10,000 =

guided_steps.say: Now divide force by area.

guided_steps.done: Back to 50 N, so p = 250,000 Pa.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm² to m² by dividing by 10,000: 2 cm² = 0.0002 m². p = 50 ÷ 0.0002 = 250,000 Pa. Dividing by 100 gives 2500.
The area must be in m². Leaving it as 2 gives 50 ÷ 2 = 25, far too small. 2 cm² = 0.0002 m².

silver.hint: Rearrange p = hρg to ρ = p ÷ (hg).
silver.display: The pressure at the bottom of a tank of liquid is 34,300 Pa. The depth is 3.5 m. Calculate the density of the liquid. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(p = h\rho g\) to \(\rho = \frac{p}{hg}\).
Divide pressure by hg.

guided_steps.done: Back to 34,300 Pa, so ρ = 1000 kg/m³.

misconceptions.message: Divide by hg, not just h: ρ = 34,300 ÷ (3.5 × 9.8) = 34,300 ÷ 34.3 = 1000 kg/m³. Dividing by 3.5 alone gives 9800.

silver.hint: Use the difference in depth, 8 − 3 metres.
silver.display: Calculate the difference in pressure between a depth of 3 m and 8 m in water (density 1000 kg/m³). (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Pressure difference depends on the CHANGE in depth: \(\Delta p = \Delta h \times \rho g\).
Multiply the depth change × density × g.

guided_steps.done: Back to 5 m of extra depth, so Δp = 49,000 Pa.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(p = h\rho g\)

misconceptions.message: Use the difference in depth: Δh = 8 − 3 = 5 m. Δp = 5 × 1000 × 9.8 = 49,000 Pa. Using 8 m gives 78,400.
